description: We’re building an interactive Martian Map for the Interplanetary Survival Guide challenge: a web app showing where humans could land, find water ice, hide from radiation and build habitats on Mars, based on real NASA data. We prototype fast with AI tools and aim for a polished demo. Looking for: a web developer, a UI/graphic designer, a Mars science or data enthusiast, and a confident presenter. Beginners welcome!
summary: S.E.R.A (Safe Exploration & Return Assistant) is a web app that plans an EVA (a walk outside the habitat) for astronauts on Mars, on the real 1 m terrain of Gale Crater, where the Curiosity rover works. The crew places the base and the science points; S.E.R.A finds a safe path over the slopes (ground steeper than 25° is closed), picks the fastest order of the points, keeps a way home from every point and checks suit time with a 15 % reserve, daylight, radio contact and live space weather from NASA DONKI and NOAA GOES. It answers one question: can we go out, and will we always get back? The answer is GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, always with the reason. Mission Twin offers a gentler second route, and a first-person helmet view lets the crew walk the plan before the EVA and test the emergency return. On Mars one mistake on the way back can cost a life; S.E.R.A makes sure every walk ends at home.
details:
What it does. S.E.R.A plans an EVA (a walk outside the habitat) on the real terrain of Gale Crater, where the Curiosity rover works. In a 2 x 2 km zone with 1 m terrain the crew places the base and up to six science points. S.E.R.A finds a safe walking path with A* (slopes of 15-25 degrees are walked twice as slowly, steeper than 25 degrees is closed), picks the fastest order of the points (checked against trying all 720 orders), keeps a way home from every point, and checks suit time (8 h with a 15 % reserve), daylight, radio contact, radiation, the dust season and live space weather (solar particle events from NASA DONKI, X-class flares from NOAA GOES). The answer is GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, always with the reason.

User experience. An interactive 3D globe leads to the landing site; a 2D map shows the route, slopes, Curiosity's real path, minerals (CRISM), geology and place names. Mission Twin compares a second, gentler route (in the demo it avoids 132 m of steep ground for +12 min). A first-person helmet view (WebGL) lets the crew walk the plan on the real terrain, see suit time and time home on the visor, test an emergency return with one button, and walk freely in Mars gravity (0.38 g) with a buddy astronaut. The guide S.E.R.A explains every step. Works on phones, offline after the first visit (PWA), in English, Russian and Uzbek.

Validity. Terrain heights match Curiosity's own record at 144 stops within 0.26 m on average; our Mars clock (solar longitude) matches 4,745 REMS weather reports within 0.77 degrees; walking speed on flat ground is 2.52 km/h (Apollo about 2.2 km/h).

Impact. One mistake on the way back can cost a life on Mars. S.E.R.A turns open NASA data into one clear decision before every walk, so every EVA ends at home. Next: any landing site, a crew of two, live suit telemetry.

Tools. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks, WebGL1 for 3D, Python for data preparation, hosted on GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/Isfandiyor-Vohidov/S.E.R.A

MRO CRISM MTRDR products via PDS Geosciences ODE
Curiosity RAD radiation (Hassler et al. 2014, Science 343)
